findings.description: setDispatcherHook rotates the dispatcher hook reference without (a) pulling outstanding mint debt from the old hook, or (b) recomputing the emission schedule. If the owner calls setDispatcherHook while the PREVIOUS hook still has outstanding mintDebt, two harmful effects compound: (1) that outstanding debt becomes unreachable because pull() is only invoked against the currently-configured dispatcherHook, so any accrued phUSD destined for this staker is effectively orphaned; (2) rewardBudget (set by the most recent _recomputeSchedule to balance + old_hook.mintDebt()) remains inflated relative to the contract's actual on-chain balance. The next user-triggered _syncBudget calls _updatePool BEFORE pull() on the new hook, decrementing the stale rewardBudget via the old rate, then attempts to pull from the new hook (which may have little-to-no debt), then recomputes. The advanced accRewardPerShare then sits above what the real balance can cover, so _safePay (which requires balance >= amount after the M-01 hardening) will revert for stakers attempting stake / unstake / claim. Users' principal remains extractable via emergencyWithdraw, but rewards accrual is effectively bricked until the owner does a corrective topUp or installs a hook with enough debt to cover the gap. The operational workaround (call pullAndRefresh() before rotating) is not enforced on-chain.
findings.attackVector: Owner (possibly a governance multisig acting routinely) rotates dispatcherHook while the old hook has non-trivial mintDebt -> previously-included V becomes unrealizable -> _updatePool continues to decrement a stale rewardBudget -> _safePay reverts on every claim/stake/unstake attempt. Not profitable for an external attacker but a realistic live-ops footgun that can freeze reward flow; must rely on emergencyWithdraw (forfeit rewards) or owner topUp to recover.
findings.recommendation: Either (1) require totalStaked == 0 before allowing a hook swap (matches the policy on setDispatcherIndex / setNFTMinter / setStakedId), or (2) call _syncBudget() to realise the old hook's mintDebt before writing the new hook reference, then call _recomputeSchedule() after — mirroring the handling in setDispatcherIndex / setNFTMinter. Additionally consider emitting a warning / requiring a non-zero hook when totalStaked > 0.

findings.description: setPauser accepts address(0) without any validation. Because the onlyPauser modifier compares msg.sender to pauser, setting pauser = address(0) effectively disables pause() / unpause() entirely (no address can produce msg.sender == 0 under the normal EVM invariants). The global Pauser registration flow expects this contract to be pausable on demand; a stale or accidental zero assignment silently breaks the emergency-pause invariant described in the parent CLAUDE.md ("pause/unpause must be callable only by the registered pauser"). Recoverable by a subsequent owner call, but there is no on-chain guard against the misconfiguration window.
findings.attackVector: Owner fat-fingers or scripts an incorrect value (e.g., an empty env variable resolving to address(0)); emergency-pause capability is silently lost. No external attacker can exploit directly, but it creates a window where a separately-discovered vulnerability cannot be mitigated via pause().
findings.recommendation: require(newPauser != address(0), "NFTStaker: zero pauser"); or explicitly document that address(0) is a deliberate "pause disabled" state and gate it behind a stronger check.

findings.description: setStakedId is gated on totalStaked == 0 and updates stakedId, but unlike its sister setters setDispatcherIndex (line 218) and setNFTMinter (line 229) it does not call _recomputeSchedule() after mutation. As a result rewardRate, rewardBudget, and windowEnd retain the values computed against the PREVIOUS token ID until the next user-triggered _syncBudget. External view functions (currentRewardRate, runwaySeconds, pendingReward, totalDebt) and off-chain integrations therefore report stale emission parameters in the interval between a setStakedId call and the first subsequent stake / claim / pullAndRefresh. No rewards are leaked (totalStaked == 0 short-circuits _updatePool) but the invariant "schedule always reflects current config once setter returns" — implicitly held by the sibling setters — is broken here, and front-end indexers driven by ScheduleRecomputed events will report an inconsistent state.
findings.attackVector: None direct. Operational / integration hazard: downstream systems querying runwaySeconds() / currentRewardRate() between setStakedId and the first recomputing interaction will see inconsistent values. The CLAUDE.md spec checklist item 6 lists setDispatcherIndex and setNFTMinter as recompute triggers but does not list setStakedId, so this may be intentional — but if so, the asymmetry with the sibling setters deserves an explicit comment.
findings.recommendation: Either call _recomputeSchedule() at the end of setStakedId (matching setDispatcherIndex / setNFTMinter) and emit ScheduleRecomputed, or add a comment documenting why this setter intentionally leaves the schedule stale.

findings.description: setDispatcherHook accepts the zero address. When dispatcherHook == address(0), _syncBudget takes the short-circuit path on line 274 (skipping pull()), which is an explicitly supported mode for owner-only topUp operation. However there is no validation that the incoming hook implements IBalancerPoolerMintDebtHook (or is even a contract). A misconfigured address will cause _syncBudget to revert at the external pull() call on every stake / unstake / claim, forcing users onto emergencyWithdraw (which forfeits pending rewards). Combined with CODE-001, this widens the freeze window.
findings.attackVector: Owner misconfiguration. Not an external-attacker vector, but meaningfully degrades the "emergencyWithdraw is the escape hatch" assurance by forcing users to forfeit rewards for what should be a routine admin operation.
findings.recommendation: Optionally validate newHook: either require address(newHook).code.length > 0 and do a low-level staticcall to mintDebt() to sanity-check the interface, or accept the current lax behaviour and surface the risk in operator runbooks.

findings.description: pendingReward mirrors _updatePool's accrual math but does NOT simulate a _syncBudget (i.e., no notional pull() on the dispatcher hook, no _recomputeSchedule). In the realistic steady state where the dispatcher hook has accrued mintDebt since the last on-chain interaction, the stored rewardRate and rewardBudget may be stale — rewardRate was set at the previous recompute against a previous V, and further elapsed time can have passed with dispatcher-side growth. A caller (UI, auto-compounder, indexer) reading pendingReward therefore gets a value that is not what claim() will actually pay them once the on-chain recompute fires. The discrepancy is typically favourable to the user (claim pays at least as much in the common case) but it is a spec-level invariant violation: the view is not an oracle for the on-chain path. Not exploitable for theft, but can mislead integrations.
findings.attackVector: None direct. Risk is misreporting to downstream callers / integrations; if an auto-compounder uses pendingReward to gate a claim, it may under- or over-trigger claims. No value at risk.
findings.recommendation: Either document the gap explicitly ("pendingReward does not simulate pull() or schedule recompute — call pullAndRefresh or interact to materialise") or add a sibling view (e.g., simulatedPendingReward) that applies the closed-form recompute against live mintDebt for accurate off-chain display.

findings.description: setNFTMinter has a zero-address guard, but there is no validation that the supplied address actually implements INFTSupply (configs(uint256) + totalSupply(uint256)). If an incorrect non-zero address is supplied, _recomputeSchedule on line 229 will revert on the configs / totalSupply calls, and all subsequent stake / unstake / claim (which call _syncBudget -> _recomputeSchedule) will revert similarly. Since the function is gated on totalStaked == 0, no principal is trapped directly, but the pool becomes unusable until the owner issues a corrective setNFTMinter. Analogous risk exists for setDispatcherIndex: an index out of bounds on the new minter will revert in _recomputeSchedule.
findings.attackVector: Owner misconfiguration. Not an external attack path.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable as-is given the totalStaked == 0 gate and the recompute-on-write that surfaces invalid minters immediately (the setter itself reverts, so the bad config is never persisted). Worth noting explicitly in the NatSpec that _recomputeSchedule doubles as a liveness probe.

findings.description: _safePay's return value is always the input amount (post-revert-check). Callers (stake, unstake, claim) re-assign the return back over the input variable, e.g. `pending = _safePay(pending);` — a no-op. After the audit M-01 hardening (revert on shortfall), the signature could drop the return value entirely without changing behaviour. Harmless but creates a false impression that the returned value might differ from the input (e.g., partial-pay semantics that no longer exist).
findings.recommendation: Either change the signature to `internal` with no return, or restore partial-pay semantics (return the actually-transferred amount, removing the revert) — the current hybrid is strictly less clear than either extreme. Given the M-01 audit rationale, dropping the return is the cleaner option.

findings.description: _recomputeSchedule is invoked from several call-sites that do NOT pre-materialise dispatcher-side mint debt (topUp, setTargetAPY, setDispatcherIndex, setNFTMinter). In those paths V on line 365-368 is computed as `balance + dispatcherHook.mintDebt()`, so rewardBudget is set to an amount strictly greater than the contract's actual token balance in the common case. Between that recompute and the next _syncBudget, _updatePool will decrement rewardBudget at the new rewardRate, advancing accRewardPerShare based on value the contract does not yet hold. _safePay enforces balance >= amount at payout time, so users cannot over-withdraw — but the side effect is that if pull() fails or yields less than the projected mintDebt, _safePay reverts and stake/unstake/claim are blocked until a topUp or working hook restores solvency. The design comment on line 331 acknowledges this rounding direction, and the parent CLAUDE.md's solvency invariant is phrased as "holds at recompute boundaries" rather than "holds always" — this is intentional, but worth noting: the invariant is BREACHED in all intervals between a recompute-without-pull and the next _syncBudget, and emergencyWithdraw is the stated escape hatch. Monitoring should alert on `_safePay` reverts to surface this state.
findings.attackVector: No theft vector (principal preserved via emergencyWithdraw, M-01 revert guards against silent forfeiture). Operational risk: reward-claim DoS whenever dispatcher-hook health degrades between a recompute-without-pull and the next _syncBudget.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) accept as-is and document the invariant-hold window explicitly in NatSpec on _recomputeSchedule, or (b) make topUp / setTargetAPY / setDispatcherIndex / setNFTMinter each call _syncBudget rather than the bare _recomputeSchedule (this would, however, couple those admin paths to dispatcher-hook liveness, defeating the explicit "dispatcher-hook-independence" design goal of topUp). Option (a) is the sane default given the explicit spec decision; the recommendation is to tighten the NatSpec on _recomputeSchedule and add an operational note to setTargetAPY.
